summary:
Article 11 of the 2008 Constitution of Ecuador binds the state to respect differences of ethnicity, nationality, social and generational standing, and gender, expressly including sexual orientation and gender identity. The provision sits within a secular, multinational constitutional order and forms the non-discrimination foundation on which LGBTI claims in Ecuador are brought.

Legal gender recognition has been available since 2016 on the basis of self-determination alone, without surgery or medical diagnosis, allowing a change of legal gender and birth name on identity documents. The National Assembly's reforms of 12 December 2023 to the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data, regulated by a decree issued by President Daniel Noboa on 11 June 2024, streamlined the civil-registry procedure through which the change is made; adults may change name and sex or gender marker directly at the civil registry, once, without a surgical requirement.

Constitutional Court rulings in 2024 and 2025 extended document changes to trans adolescents and publicly rebuked the National Assembly for stalling implementation of trans-rights legislation. An April 2026 report describes the adolescent ruling as opening a path for others seeking legal recognition.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1997, when Constitutional Tribunal Case No. 111-97-TC struck Article 516 of the Penal Code, and the 1998 Constitution made Ecuador the first country in the Americas to bar discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation. Conversion practices are criminalised as torture under Article 151 of the Penal Code, in force since 2014 and carrying 7 to 10 years' imprisonment, although as of 2023 hundreds of clinics were still promoting them.

Violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians rose amid the internal armed conflict, according to a January 2024 report. A 2011 United States State Department human-rights report found discrimination by public and private bodies against gay, lesbian and transgender people, and recorded LGBT group claims that police and prosecutors did not thoroughly investigate deaths of LGBT individuals; the same report found the right to equal access to formal education frequently violated.

Detention is the sharpest documented harm. Trans women in Ecuador are held almost without exception in male prison spaces, where they report gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and barriers to health care. Helen Maldonado, a trans woman, died during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space; in 2026 a 23-year-old trans woman died in state custody at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison, prompting calls for an independent investigation.

Family recognition is partial. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2019, and in 2018 the Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register the daughter of a same-sex couple, a precedent for state recognition of same-sex families. Adoption is constitutionally restricted to different-sex couples under Article 68, and legislation passed on 14 August 2026 by 118 votes to 0 explicitly prohibits single and same-sex couples from adopting.
tangentialFactors:
Ecuador's framework is among the more developed in the region on paper: self-determination-based legal gender recognition dating from 2016, explicit constitutional protection of gender identity since 1998, and criminalisation of conversion practices as torture sit alongside marriage equality. The gap between that framework and conditions of detention, where trans women are housed by birth sex and die in custody, is the defining pattern.

The internal armed conflict and the associated rise in violence reported in January 2024 form the wider security background against which LGBTQ people move, and reportage links the deterioration in safety to that context rather than to any change in the legal position.

Societal attitudes are described as conservative and macho, with homosexuality commonly viewed negatively, while public visibility is nonetheless permitted: pride marches have been authorised in all major cities with police protection and official participation, drawing roughly 20,000 attendees in Guayaquil in 2017 and over 18,000 in Quito in 2018, with public buildings lit in rainbow colours on occasion.

Public officials have faced legal consequences for anti-gay speech: presidential candidate Nelson Zavala was fined over $3,000 and barred from office for a year in 2013 for describing gay people as sinners and immoral. Diane Marie Rodríguez Zambrano became the first openly transgender candidate in 2013 and the first transgender lawmaker in 2017.
localsOnly:
Residents change name and marker once, directly at the civil registry, under the December 2023 reforms as regulated on 11 June 2024; the procedure does not require surgery. Whether the same route is available to a person present in Ecuador without civil status there is not addressed by the sources.

Prison placement for trans women operates on birth sex and legal sex. The last prison census counted 73 trans women across all Ecuadorian prisons, a figure the organisation Fundación Vivir Libre says undercounts; most are held in male pavilions. A 'prioritaria' pavilion reserved for vulnerable populations holds many gender-diverse detainees, but placement there is used unevenly. A Venezuelan trans woman detained in August 2023 at Penitenciaria del Litoral was sent to a male pavilion with three other trans women rather than the prioritaria unit, and received no medical examinations or HIV treatment there. A 2022 complaint alleged cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio, and 2024 allegations included forced head-shaving, beatings and violence targeting breast and body implants.

The PrisioTrans programme of Silueta X documents these cases from 2011 to 2026 and does not press a single placement rule. It advocates individualised housing decisions under Inter-American standards that weigh gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, and cites a July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty.

Article 68 of the Constitution limits adoption to different-sex couples, and the law passed on 14 August 2026 by 118 to 0 extends that exclusion to single people as well as same-sex couples. The 2018 order registering the daughter of a lesbian couple, decided 5-3 with one abstention, remains the countervailing precedent on family recognition.

Conversion practices carry 7 to 10 years' imprisonment under Article 151 as of 2014, yet hundreds of clinics were still promoting them in 2023. The 2011 rights report also recorded clinics confining young people against their will, including the daughter of parents who unsuccessfully sought her release, and persistent discrimination in access to formal education.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry, visa and border-screening rules for transgender visitors, including the treatment of gender markers on foreign passports, are not covered by any source in this inventory; no finding on entry screening can be made from the material available.

Facilities access, such as restroom and changing arrangements in schools, workplaces or public buildings, is not sourced. Nor is access to gender-affirming healthcare for a person visiting Ecuador, outside the documented refusal of medical care to a detained trans woman.

The inventory does not establish whether Ecuador's criminal law contains a hate-crime or aggravated-sentence provision for offences motivated by gender identity, beyond the conversion-practices provision and general constitutional non-discrimination. Nor does it source a specific anti-discrimination statute with a complaints mechanism.

The prison census figure of 73 trans women is contested by advocates who say the true number is far higher, so the scale of exposure remains unresolved. The 2026 death at El Encuentro was, at the time of the source, the subject of calls for an independent investigation rather than a completed one, and no outcome is recorded.

The sources do not state whether the 2024 and 2025 Constitutional Court rulings on adolescent document changes are final, appealable or contingent on implementing legislation, nor whether the June 2024 regulation has been amended since issuance.
